title: Warfarin INR: Targets, Lupus Anticoagulant Pitfalls and Superwarfarin Poisoning
summary: Learn how the INR is calculated, which INR range fits atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism and mechanical valves, why a lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise the INR, and why brodifacoum poisoning needs months of vitamin K.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 39 Hit 1 (warfarin INR targets and INR formula), Hit 6 (brodifacoum poisoning) and Exam Trap 2 (lupus anticoagulant and a falsely high INR). The caged-ball aortic range (2.5–3.5) is taught from the Indian 2019 guideline table; single targets of 3.0 for caged-ball and 2.5 for AF and the mean INR of about 15 were not found in the sources read and are not taught. The chromogenic factor X assay is taught as a limited alternative, not as the routine replacement the trap implies. Brodifacoum half-life and vitamin K duration are taught as ranges from specific studies. Targets come from US (ACCP) and Indian guidance; Philippine guidance is not covered. Not taught: Number Vault table, DOAC reversal, TEG heparinase cup.

objectives: Calculate the INR from the patient PT, the mean normal PT and the ISI, and state what it is standardised for.
State the usual INR range for atrial fibrillation and VTE and the guideline targets for mechanical aortic and mitral valves.
Explain how a lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise the INR and list the laboratory options.
Recognise brodifacoum poisoning and explain why vitamin K is continued after the INR normalises.

scenes.title: Three INRs, three stories
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three INR results reach the coagulation bench — (1) a patient with atrial fibrillation on warfarin, INR 2.6; (2) a patient with antiphospholipid syndrome on warfarin whose point-of-care INR reads 3.4, yet a new clot has formed; (3) a young man with no prescribed anticoagulant, blood in the urine and an INR above 10 after smoking synthetic cannabinoids. Question token: “On target, falsely high, or poison?”

cues.text: Three INR results arrive. A patient with atrial fibrillation on warfarin has an INR of two point six.

A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome reads three point four on a fingerstick meter, yet has a new clot. And a young man on no anticoagulant has blood in his urine and an INR above ten after smoking synthetic cannabinoids.
Which INR is on target, which one may be falsely high, and which one is a poisoning?

props.label: On target, falsely high, or poison?

scenes.title: What the INR measures
scenes.altText: Schematic: the vitamin K cycle and a PT tube. Mechanism card: vitamin K antagonists (warfarin and the long-acting rodenticides) inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, so factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C, S, Z) are not carboxylated. PT card: the prothrombin time clots plasma with a thromboplastin reagent. Formula card: INR = (patient PT / MNPT)^ISI; MNPT is the geometric mean PT of at least 20 healthy volunteers; ISI describes the reagent’s sensitivity relative to the WHO reference; a local ISI for the reagent–analyser pair is preferred. Scope token: the INR improves comparability mainly in patients on vitamin K antagonists.

cues.text: Warfarin and its long-acting rodenticide cousins block vitamin K epoxide reductase. Without recycled vitamin K, the liver cannot activate factors two, seven, nine and ten.
The prothrombin time clots the plasma with a thromboplastin reagent. But reagents differ in sensitivity, so raw seconds cannot be compared between laboratories.

The INR fixes that. Divide the patient’s PT by the mean normal PT, the geometric mean of at least twenty healthy people, and raise the ratio to the power of the reagent’s international sensitivity index.
This standardisation was built for patients on vitamin K antagonists, and that is where it works best.

props.title: VKOR blocked
lines: II, VII, IX, X not activated

scenes.title: Targets depend on the indication
scenes.altText: Target card (ACCP 9th edition and Anticoagulation Forum guidance): atrial fibrillation, INR range 2.0–3.0; venous thromboembolism, 2.0–3.0 with a target of 2.5 (ACCP VTE guideline). Valve card (ACCP 2012): mechanical aortic valve, target 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0); mechanical mitral valve, target 3.0 (range 2.5–3.5); mechanical aortic plus mitral valves, target 3.0 (2.5–3.5). Risk token (Indian 2019 guideline and its summary table): caged-ball aortic valve, and mechanical aortic valve with risk factors (atrial fibrillation, previous thromboembolism, left ventricular dysfunction, hypercoagulable state), 2.5–3.5. Caution token: targets are guideline-dependent; follow the current local guideline.

cues.text: The INR target depends on why the patient takes warfarin. For atrial fibrillation and for venous thromboembolism, the usual range is two to three; the chest physicians’ clot guideline names two point five as the target.

Mechanical valves are different. The 2012 chest physicians’ guideline targets two point five, range two to three, for a mechanical aortic valve, and three, range two point five to three point five, for a mechanical mitral valve or for valves in both positions.

The aortic range can be higher too. An Indian guideline lists two point five to three point five for an older caged-ball aortic valve, and for a mechanical aortic valve with risk factors such as atrial fibrillation, previous clots or a weak left ventricle.

So an INR of two point six is on target for atrial fibrillation, but for a mechanical mitral valve it sits only just inside the range, below the target of three. Targets are guideline-dependent: always check the current local guideline.

scenes.title: When the INR misleads
scenes.altText: Left card, lupus anticoagulant: antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with phospholipid-based clotting tests; a lupus anticoagulant can react with the thromboplastin and falsely raise the INR, masking a subtherapeutic dose; more often with point-of-care devices. Fixes: choose a thromboplastin less sensitive to the antibodies; a chromogenic factor X assay is thromboplastin-independent but not widely available, may take days, and has no established therapeutic range. Right card, brodifacoum: a long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide about 100 times more potent than warfarin; half-lives reported from about 7.5 days to 16–36 days (up to 62); high-dose vitamin K1 (25–600 mg/day) for weeks to months; one cohort median 140 days (range 28–730); confirmed by HPLC or LC-MS/MS; a normal INR at discharge does not mean the drug has gone.

cues.text: Patient two. Antiphospholipid antibodies can react with the thromboplastin and falsely raise the INR, hiding a dose that is really too low. Point-of-care meters are more often affected.

Choose a thromboplastin less sensitive to the antibodies. A chromogenic factor ten assay avoids thromboplastin altogether, but it is not widely available, can take days, and has no established target range.

Patient three. Brodifacoum, a long-acting rodenticide, is about a hundred times more potent than warfarin, and its reported half-life ranges from about a week to more than a month. Chromatography with mass spectrometry confirms it.
Treatment needs high-dose vitamin K one for weeks to months; one cohort needed a median of a hundred and forty days. A normal INR at discharge does not mean the poison has gone.

props.title: Brodifacoum
lines: Vitamin K1 for weeks to months

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A high INR in a warfarin patient always means overdose” (✓ in antiphospholipid syndrome, a lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise it, especially on meters); “Every warfarin patient targets 2–3” (✓ a mechanical mitral valve targets 3.0, range 2.5–3.5); “The INR is normal, so stop vitamin K after brodifacoum” (✓ brodifacoum outlasts the INR; continue vitamin K for weeks to months).

cues.text: Trap one: a high INR on warfarin always means overdose. No: in antiphospholipid syndrome, a lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise it.
Trap two: every warfarin patient targets two to three. No: a mechanical mitral valve targets three, range two point five to three point five.
Trap three: the INR is normal, so stop vitamin K after brodifacoum. No: the poison outlasts the INR, so treatment continues for weeks to months.

props.title: ✗ “High INR = overdose.”
lines: ✓ Lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise it

scenes.title: Ruler, static, slow tank
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The INR is a RULER with marks set by the indication (2–3 for most, 2.5–3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve); a lupus anticoagulant is STATIC on the line that makes the ruler read long; brodifacoum is a SLOW-LEAKING TANK that keeps refilling the problem after the gauge looks normal.” Tokens: ruler = targets · static = lupus anticoagulant · slow tank = brodifacoum. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the INR is a ruler whose marks are set by the indication. A lupus anticoagulant is static on the line that makes the ruler read long. Brodifacoum is a slow-leaking tank that keeps the problem going after the gauge looks normal.

Where it breaks: the ruler is only standardised for vitamin K antagonists; the static depends on the reagent and device, and some reagents barely pick it up; and the tank does not drain at one predictable rate, because reported half-lives vary widely.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: INR standardised only for VKA patients
LA effect is reagent- and device-dependent

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “INR 2–3 for atrial fibrillation and VTE · mechanical mitral 3.0 (2.5–3.5)”, “Lupus anticoagulant can falsely raise the INR · brodifacoum outlasts a normal INR”.

cues.text: Judge a warfarin INR against the target for that indication, suspect a lupus anticoagulant when a high INR and a new clot disagree, and keep giving vitamin K after brodifacoum poisoning because the poison outlasts a normal INR.

props.label: LA can falsely raise INR · brodifacoum outlasts a normal INR

explanation.what: Plain language: warfarin stops the liver from finishing four clotting factors, and the INR is a standardised way of reporting how slowly the blood clots on it. The right INR depends on why the patient takes warfarin. Some antibodies make the test read too high, and some rat poisons act like a much stronger, much longer-lasting warfarin. Scientific terms: vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), factors II, VII, IX and X, prothrombin time (PT), thromboplastin, mean normal prothrombin time (MNPT), international sensitivity index (ISI), international normalized ratio (INR), lupus anticoagulant (LA), antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), chromogenic factor X (CFX), long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (LAAR), brodifacoum, vitamin K1 (phytonadione).
explanation.why: Reagents differ in sensitivity, so the INR raises the PT ratio to the ISI to make results comparable for patients on vitamin K antagonists. Guidelines set a higher target for a mechanical mitral valve, which ACCP and Indian risk tables place in the high thrombotic-risk group along with caged-ball aortic valves. Antiphospholipid antibodies interfere with phospholipid-dependent clotting tests, so a lupus anticoagulant can lengthen the PT and hide an inadequate dose. Brodifacoum is highly potent and lipophilic, has little liver metabolism and recirculates enterohepatically, so it outlasts the vitamin K given and the coagulopathy returns if treatment stops too early.
explanation.measure: INR = (patient PT / MNPT)^ISI; MNPT = geometric mean PT of at least 20 healthy volunteers; a local ISI for the reagent–analyser pair is preferred. Atrial fibrillation and VTE: INR 2.0–3.0 (ACCP VTE target 2.5). ACCP 2012: mechanical aortic valve, target 2.5 (2.0–3.0); mechanical mitral or both positions, target 3.0 (2.5–3.5). Indian 2019 guideline: caged-ball aortic valve, or mechanical aortic valve with risk factors, 2.5–3.5. Brodifacoum: about 100 times as potent as warfarin; reported half-lives about 7.5 days to 16–36 days (rarely 62); vitamin K1 25–600 mg/day; one cohort median 140 days (range 28–730); safe plasma level below 10 ng/mL; confirmed by HPLC or LC-MS/MS.
explanation.differs: True overanticoagulation vs LA-related false elevation (a high INR that can mask a subtherapeutic dose, reagent- and device-dependent); warfarin (short-acting, about 10 mg vitamin K or less reverses it) vs brodifacoum (very long-acting, very large vitamin K doses for weeks to months); INR (thromboplastin-dependent) vs chromogenic factor X (thromboplastin-independent but limited availability and no established range).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate an INR, choose the target for a given indication or valve, explain an apparently therapeutic INR with a new clot in APS, or decide what to do when a brodifacoum patient’s INR normalises.

questions.stem: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve is on warfarin. Under the 2012 ACCP guideline, which INR target and range apply?

options.rationale: Correct. ACCP 2012 suggests this for a mechanical mitral valve (and for valves in both positions).
Incorrect. This is the ACCP target for a mechanical aortic valve, not a mitral one.
Incorrect. This is below every warfarin target discussed for mechanical valves.
Incorrect. The guideline does not recommend this high range.

questions.stem: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome on warfarin has a new venous clot, although a point-of-care INR reads 3.4. What is the best laboratory explanation and response?

options.text: The lupus anticoagulant may be falsely raising the INR; recheck with a less LA-sensitive thromboplastin or an LA-independent test such as chromogenic factor X
options.rationale: Correct. LA can react with the thromboplastin and mask a subtherapeutic dose; meters are more often affected, and chromogenic factor X does not use thromboplastin.

options.text: The patient is overanticoagulated; stop warfarin
options.rationale: Incorrect. A new clot with a high INR suggests the INR may be misleading, not that the dose is too high.

options.text: The INR proves therapeutic anticoagulation, so the clot must be a treatment failure
options.rationale: Incorrect. Recurrence should first be checked against a reliable INR, because LA can give a spuriously therapeutic value.
Incorrect. LA also prolongs the APTT, so switching to it does not remove the interference; the options sources give are a less LA-sensitive thromboplastin or chromogenic factor X.

questions.stem: A patient treated for brodifacoum poisoning has an INR of 1.2 on day 5 of high-dose vitamin K1. What should happen next?

options.text: Continue vitamin K1 for weeks to months, monitoring the INR and, where available, plasma brodifacoum
options.rationale: Correct. Brodifacoum persists long after the INR normalises; stopping early risks recurrent coagulopathy.

options.text: Stop vitamin K1 because the INR is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. In one series most patients had a normal INR at discharge while plasma brodifacoum was still far above the safe level.

options.text: Switch to a single 10 mg dose of vitamin K, as for warfarin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Brodifacoum is far more potent; doses of 25–600 mg per day have been needed.

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma alone and stop vitamin K
options.rationale: Incorrect. Factors given in PCC or plasma have a limited half-life, so vitamin K must be continued for the liver to keep making functional factors.

claims.text: INR = (PT/MNPT)^ISI; MNPT from at least 20 healthy volunteers; local ISI preferred; INR standardised mainly for VKA patients.
VKAs and LAARs inhibit VKOR, leaving factors II, VII, IX and X uncarboxylated.

AF and VTE INR 2.0–3.0 (VTE target 2.5); ACCP 2012 mechanical aortic 2.5 (2.0–3.0), mitral and double 3.0 (2.5–3.5); Indian 2019 caged-ball aortic and aortic with risk factors 2.5–3.5; mitral and caged-ball aortic prostheses high thrombotic risk.

LA can falsely raise the INR and mask underdosing, more often on point-of-care devices; choose less sensitive reagents; chromogenic factor X is thromboplastin-independent but limited (availability, turnaround, no established range).

Brodifacoum about 100 times as potent as warfarin; half-lives about 7.5 days to 16–36 days (rarely 62); vitamin K1 25–600 mg/day for weeks to months; median 140 days (28–730) in one cohort; HPLC or LC-MS/MS confirmation; normal INR at discharge with persisting drug.
A single target of 3.0 for caged-ball aortic valves; a single target of 2.5 for atrial fibrillation; mean INR of about 15 in brodifacoum poisoning.
claims.note: Not found in the sources read (Saksena gives a caged-ball range only; the ACCP AF guideline portion read gives a range only); not taught as facts.

claims.text: Scenario invented; vitamin K cycle drawing schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 39 Hit 1 gives INR 2–3 (target 2.5) for AF and VTE and 2.5–3.5 (target 3.0) for mechanical mitral and older caged-ball aortic valves. The ranges are supported (ACCP 2012; Indian 2019 table: caged-ball aortic 2.5–3.5), and the ACCP VTE guideline names target 2.5; but the caged-ball source gives a range only (no 3.0 target), the ACCP AF guideline portion read gives a range only, and the Indian guideline also raises a mechanical aortic valve with risk factors to 2.5–3.5. Targets are guideline-dependent (US ACCP and Indian guidance read; Philippine guidance not covered) (register flag rv-ch39-inr-valve-targets).

Ch. 39 Exam Trap 2 says to use a chromogenic factor X assay to monitor warfarin instead when a lupus anticoagulant is present. Sources first advise choosing a thromboplastin less sensitive to the antibodies and describe chromogenic factor X as an alternative that is not widely available, may take several days, and has no established therapeutic range (register flag rv-ch39-cfx-limited).

Ch. 39 Hit 6 gives brodifacoum INR mean ~15, half-life 16–36 days and vitamin K1 for a median of 140 days (up to 730) as general figures. Hong 2010 attributes the 16–36-day half-life to a three-case study (Kodali 2019 gives it as the usual range); other reports give about 7.5 days in the 2018 synthetic-cannabinoid patients and rarely up to 62 days; the 140-day median (range 28–730) comes from one 24-patient cohort; a mean INR of 15 was not found (Illinois index patients ranged from 5 to above 20) (register flag rv-ch39-brodifacoum-figures).

morphology.note: No images; the vitamin K cycle, tests and drugs are shown as cards.

verification.notes: 5 factual claims checked against ACCP 2012 AF, VTE and valve guidelines (read via a page-fetch tool), Saksena 2019, Witt 2016, Bronić 2019, Zou 2026, Sayar 2021, Capecchi 2022, Greenmyer 2021, Bahouth 2019, Hong 2010, Kodali 2019, Nosal 2021, Long 2016 and Moritz 2018; 1 pending (single 3.0 target for caged-ball valves, single 2.5 target for AF, mean brodifacoum INR 15), not taught.
